lessons.title: Nutrient Uptake Patterns in Onions
lessons.body: Onions have a shallow root system, mostly in the top 15-20 cm of soil, so they need nutrients close by and available. Uptake is slow for the first 30-40 days after transplanting or sowing. Then from about day 40 to day 80, the plants take up nutrients rapidly as leaves and bulbs form. After day 80, uptake slows down as bulbs mature. For a 1-hectare crop aiming for 20-30 tonnes of bulbs, onions remove roughly 100-120 kg nitrogen (N), 40-50 kg phosphorus (P2O5), and 80-100 kg potassium (K2O). They also need calcium, magnesium, sulphur, and micronutrients like zinc and boron. In African soils, nitrogen and phosphorus are often low, while potassium may be adequate in some volcanic soils but low in sandy soils. A soil test before planting is your best guide. If you cannot test, a common recommendation for onion in West Africa is 100 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 80 kg K2O per hectare, split into 2-3 applications. Onions are sensitive to salt, so do not dump all fertilizer at once. Also, onions have a small root volume, so banding fertilizer 5-10 cm beside the plant row is better than broadcasting. During bulb formation, potassium and sulphur are critical for bulb size, firmness, and storage life. Too much nitrogen late in the season delays maturity and causes thick necks, which rot in storage. So match your fertilizer to the uptake curve: light at start, heavy during rapid growth, and stop nitrogen 3-4 weeks before harvest. This pattern works whether you use organic or mineral fertilizers. In sandy soils, nutrients leach quickly, so split applications are even more important. In heavy clay, roots may struggle, so ensure good soil structure. Always water after applying fertilizer to dissolve it and move it into the root zone. Remember, onions are poor competitors with weeds, so a healthy crop with balanced nutrition will also shade the soil and reduce weed pressure. Start with a soil test, follow the uptake pattern, and you will get bigger, better bulbs.

lessons.title: Split Fertilizer Applications
lessons.body: Onions need fertilizer in small, frequent doses because their roots are shallow and they cannot take up large amounts at once. Split application means dividing the total fertilizer into 2-4 parts and applying them at different growth stages. For a 1-hectare crop, if your total is 100 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 80 kg K2O, you could apply: at planting (basal), 30 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 40 kg K2O; at 4-6 weeks after transplanting, 40 kg N and 20 kg K2O; at 8-10 weeks, 30 kg N and 20 kg K2O. This matches the onion's uptake curve. In Africa, common fertilizers are urea (46% N), NPK 15-15-15, and muriate of potash (60% K2O). For the basal, you can use NPK 15-15-15: to supply 30 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 40 kg K2O, you would need about 200 kg of NPK 15-15-15 (which gives 30 kg N, 30 kg P2O5, 30 kg K2O) plus additional 30 kg P2O5 from single superphosphate (about 170 kg) and 10 kg K2O from muriate of potash (about 17 kg). That is complicated, so many farmers use a simpler approach: apply 200 kg NPK 15-15-15 at planting, then top-dress with 100 kg urea at 4 weeks and another 100 kg urea at 8 weeks. That gives roughly 30 kg N from NPK plus 46 kg N from first urea and 46 kg N from second urea, total 122 kg N, which is close. Adjust based on your soil test. Split application reduces nutrient loss through leaching and volatilization, especially in sandy soils or high rainfall. It also prevents salt burn to young seedlings. Apply fertilizer in a band 5-10 cm from the plant row and cover lightly with soil, then irrigate. Do not apply on wet leaves; urea can burn them. If you use organic manure, split it too: incorporate well-rotted manure before planting and side-dress with compost or poultry litter at 4 weeks. Splitting is more work but pays off with higher yield and better bulb quality. It also saves money because less fertilizer is wasted. Always keep records of what you apply and when, so you can improve next season.

lessons.title: Foliar Feeding for Quick Correction
lessons.body: Foliar feeding means spraying liquid fertilizer directly onto onion leaves. It is a fast way to correct nutrient deficiencies because nutrients enter through the leaf within hours, not days. Use it when you see symptoms like yellowing (nitrogen), purple tips (phosphorus), or leaf edge burn (potassium). Foliar feeding is not a substitute for soil fertilization, but a supplement for quick fixes. For onions, common foliar sprays are urea (2-3% solution, i.e., 20-30 g per litre of water), potassium nitrate (1-2%), or commercial micronutrient mixes. To make a 2% urea solution, dissolve 200 g of urea in 10 litres of water. Spray in the early morning or late evening to avoid leaf burn from midday sun. Add a few drops of liquid soap as a sticker to help the spray stick to the waxy onion leaves. Spray until leaves are wet but not dripping. Do not spray if rain is expected within 6 hours. For micronutrient deficiencies like zinc or boron, use chelated products at recommended rates, often 1-2 g per litre. Boron is needed in very small amounts; too much is toxic, so measure carefully. Foliar feeding is especially useful during bulb formation when roots may be less active, or after heavy rain when soil nutrients leached. In Africa, many farmers use foliar sprays based on local materials: e.g., wood ash soaked in water (provides potassium) or compost tea (provides a range of nutrients). To make compost tea, put 1 part mature compost in 5 parts water, let it steep for 3-5 days, strain, and dilute 1:5 before spraying. This is a gentle, organic option. Always test a small area first to check for leaf burn. If you see burning, dilute more. Foliar sprays can also be mixed with some pesticides, but check compatibility. Do not mix with alkaline substances like lime. For best results, spray every 7-10 days during rapid growth if deficiency persists, but no more than 3-4 times per season. Remember, foliar feeding is a rescue tool, not a full feeding program. Use it wisely and combine with good soil management.

lessons.title: Organic Fertilizers and Amendments
lessons.body: Organic fertilizers come from plant or animal sources: manure, compost, poultry litter, green manures, and crop residues. They release nutrients slowly, improve soil structure, and increase water-holding capacity. For onions, well-rotted cattle manure is a good base. Apply 10-20 tonnes per hectare (about 1-2 kg per square metre) and incorporate into the top 15 cm of soil 2-4 weeks before planting. Fresh manure can burn roots and carry weed seeds, so always compost it first. Poultry litter is richer: apply 5-10 tonnes per hectare. Compost made from kitchen waste, crop residues, and animal manure is excellent. To make compost, layer green and brown materials, keep it moist, and turn every 2 weeks. It is ready in 6-8 weeks when dark and crumbly. In Africa, other organic amendments include wood ash (potassium and calcium), bone meal (phosphorus), and blood meal (nitrogen). Wood ash can be applied at 200-500 kg per hectare, but do not use too much as it raises soil pH. Bone meal is slow-release; apply 200-400 kg per hectare before planting. Blood meal is fast-acting nitrogen; apply 100-200 kg per hectare as a side-dress. Green manures like cowpea or mucuna can be grown before onions and ploughed in to add nitrogen. Organic matter also feeds soil microbes that help onions take up nutrients. However, organic fertilizers alone may not supply enough nutrients for high yields. Combine them with mineral fertilizers. For example, apply manure at planting plus a split of urea. This integrated approach is common in African market gardens. Also, consider biochar: charred organic matter that improves soil fertility and water retention. Apply 1-2 tonnes per hectare. Always test your manure or compost for nutrient content if possible; otherwise, use general recommendations. Store manure under cover to prevent nutrient loss from rain and sun. Do not apply manure to onions close to harvest because of food safety concerns. With organic amendments, you build soil health for the long term while feeding your onions now.

lessons.title: Preventing Nutrient Deficiencies
lessons.body: Preventing deficiencies is easier and cheaper than curing them. Start with a soil test. In many African countries, soil testing services are available through agricultural extension offices or private labs. A basic test costs about $20-50 and tells you pH, organic matter, and available N, P, K, and micronutrients. Adjust pH to 6.0-6.8 for onions; if too acidic (below 5.5), apply agricultural lime at 1-2 tonnes per hectare. If too alkaline (above 7.5), add gypsum or elemental sulphur. Use a balanced fertilizer program based on test results. Common deficiency symptoms: nitrogen deficiency shows as pale green to yellow older leaves; phosphorus deficiency gives purple leaf tips and stunted growth; potassium deficiency causes leaf edge burn and small bulbs; calcium deficiency leads to leaf tip dieback and poor bulb storage; magnesium deficiency shows yellowing between veins on older leaves; sulphur deficiency looks like nitrogen but on younger leaves. Zinc deficiency causes stunted plants with yellow bands on leaves; boron deficiency leads to hollow stems and brown spots on bulbs. To prevent these, apply a complete fertilizer at planting, then split nitrogen and potassium. For micronutrients, use a soil application of zinc sulphate (10-20 kg/ha) or borax (10-15 kg/ha) if deficient. Foliar sprays can correct quickly. Organic matter helps prevent deficiencies by holding nutrients and releasing them slowly. Crop rotation with cereals or legumes reduces pest and disease buildup and balances nutrient use. Avoid over-irrigation, which leaches nitrogen and sulphur. Keep weeds down because they compete for nutrients. Monitor your crop weekly. If you see early symptoms, act fast. Keep a notebook to record what you see and what you apply. This helps you learn your farm's patterns. In sandy soils, deficiencies are more common because nutrients leach; in clay soils, nutrients may be locked up. So adjust your management. Also, consider using slow-release fertilizers or coated urea to reduce losses. For organic growers, regular additions of compost and manure prevent most deficiencies. Remember, healthy soil grows healthy onions. Prevention is a season-long effort, not a one-time fix.

lessons.title: Fertigation: Injecting Fertilizers via Irrigation
lessons.body: Fertigation is the practice of injecting soluble fertilizers into irrigation water. It is common in drip irrigation but can also be used with sprinklers or even watering cans. For onions, fertigation saves fertilizer, reduces labor, and delivers nutrients exactly when the plant needs them. You need a fertilizer tank, a injector (venturi or pump), and soluble fertilizers like potassium nitrate, calcium nitrate, urea, and monoammonium phosphate. Do not use granular fertilizers that do not dissolve; they will clog emitters. A simple setup for a small farm: a 200-litre drum, a tap, and a hose connected to a drip line. Mix fertilizer in the drum, let it dissolve, and let it flow into the irrigation water at a controlled rate. For a 1-hectare drip system, you can inject 5-10 kg of fertilizer per 1000 litres of water, depending on your schedule. A common fertigation schedule for onions: week 3-4 after transplanting: 20 kg N, 10 kg P2O5, 20 kg K2O per hectare per week; week 5-8: 25 kg N, 5 kg P2O5, 25 kg K2O per week; week 9-12: 15 kg N, 0 P2O5, 30 kg K2O per week. That totals roughly 100 kg N, 30 kg P2O5, 100 kg K2O. Adjust based on soil test. Always inject fertilizers after the system is full of water, and flush with clean water for 10-15 minutes after injection to prevent salt buildup in the lines. Do not mix calcium fertilizers with phosphate or sulphate fertilizers; they form precipitates that clog emitters. Inject them separately, with a flush in between. Fertigation is efficient but requires careful management. Test the EC (electrical conductivity) of your solution; for onions, keep it below 2.0 dS/m to avoid salt burn. If you see leaf edge burn, reduce concentration. In Africa, fertigation is gaining popularity among commercial onion growers, especially in Kenya, South Africa, and Egypt. For smallholders, a simple bucket drip system can be used. Always use clean water and filter it. Keep records of what you inject and when. Fertigation can increase yields by 20-30% compared to broadcasting, because nutrients are placed right in the root zone. It also reduces weed growth because only the crop gets water and nutrients. However, it requires investment in equipment and regular maintenance. If you are not ready for fertigation, split soil applications are the next best thing.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Fertilization & Nutrient Management for Onion Farming in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the core nutrient-management decisions an African onion grower must make across a season. It is written for commercial and semi-commercial producers who sell into urban markets, supermarkets, hotels, and regional trade corridors â where bulb size, uniformity, skin quality, and shelf life determine price. Onions are a shallow-rooted, low-tolerance crop: they demand steady but modest nutrition, and they punish both under- and over-feeding. The goal of this module is profitable, consistent marketable yield, not maximum biomass.

Onion roots rarely exceed 30 cm depth and have limited root-hair density, so they cannot scavenge nutrients efficiently. This is why placement, timing, and split applications matter more in onions than in maize or cassava. A dollar spent on fertilizer at the wrong growth stage is largely wasted; the same dollar split across the right stages can raise marketable yield by 20â40%.

1. Nutrient Uptake Patterns in Onions

Onion nutrient demand is low during establishment, rises sharply during active leaf growth (roughly 30â60 days after transplanting), peaks at bulb initiation and early bulbing, then declines as the tops fall over. Nitrogen (N) drives leaf area and bulb size; phosphorus (P) supports root and early establishment; potassium (K) governs bulb size, dry matter, firmness, and storage life. Sulphur (S) is critical for pungency and flavour compounds in Allium crops, and calcium plus boron reduce the risk of split and thick-neck bulbs.

Practical implication: place all P and most K at planting, then split N across two or three applications. Onions respond to N up to about 120â150 kg N/ha on most African soils, but exceeding this delays maturity, produces thick necks, and reduces storage life â a direct business loss for growers who store bulbs for off-season sales.

2. Split Fertilizer Applications

Split application matches supply to demand and reduces leaching, especially on sandy or irrigated soils common in Kenya's Kajiado, Tanzania's Kilimanjaro lowlands, and Nigeria's Kano River irrigation schemes. A workable three-way split for a 120 kg N/ha programme:

Table 1. Recommended split N and K schedule for irrigated bulb onion (per hectare)
Stage Timing N (kg/ha) KâO (kg/ha) Notes
Basal / transplanting 0â5 days 30 60 All P (as DAP or TSP) plus K
Vegetative 25â35 days 45 30 Top-dress with CAN or urea
Bulb initiation 50â60 days 45 30 Stop N after 70 days
Bulb fill (optional) 70â80 days 0 20 K only, via fertigation or foliar

Sources: FAO, Onion Cultivation and Post-Harvest Handling; AVRDC/WorldVeg onion production guides; KALRO (Kenya) horticulture recommendations.

3. Foliar Feeding for Quick Correction

Foliar sprays correct visible deficiencies within 3â7 days and are invaluable when soil conditions (dry, waterlogged, high pH) block root uptake. They are a corrective tool, not a replacement for a soil-based programme. Typical African use cases: micronutrient deficiencies on high-pH soils (calcareous or sodic patches), calcium deficiency causing leaf-tip dieback, and rapid K top-up during bulbing.

Table 2. Common foliar treatments for onion (per 100 L water)
Nutrient Product & rate Target stage Frequency
Calcium + Boron Ca(NOâ)â 1â2 kg + solubor 50 g Bulb initiation 2 sprays, 10 days apart
Potassium KNOâ 1.5â2 kg Bulb fill 2â3 sprays
Zinc ZnSOâ 200â300 g Vegetative 1â2 sprays
Iron (chelate) Fe-EDDHA 50â80 g Early vegetative 1â2 sprays

Sources: University of California ANR, Onion Nutrient Management; KALRO / KEPHIS extension bulletins; FAO fertilizer use manuals.

4. Organic Fertilizers and Amendments

Well-decomposed cattle, poultry, or goat manure at 10â20 t/ha supplies slow-release nutrients, improves water-holding on sandy soils, and boosts microbial activity. Compost and vermicompost at 5â10 t/ha are cost-effective where manure is scarce. In acidic East African highland soils (pH < 5.5), agricultural lime at 2â4 t/ha applied 4â6 weeks before planting raises pH and unlocks P and Ca. In sodic irrigated zones (parts of Kano, Senegal River Valley), gypsum (CaSOâ) at 2â5 t/ha is the corrective amendment. Organic sources are not a stand-alone strategy for high-yield onions â combine them with mineral fertilizer for best returns.

5. Preventing Nutrient Deficiencies

Prevention is cheaper than correction. Start with a soil test every 2â3 seasons (KALRO, NARO, and national extension labs offer this at low cost). Maintain soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8. Rotate with cereals or legumes â never plant onion after onion, garlic, or leek. Keep irrigation steady; drought stress concentrates salts and induces Ca and B disorders. Watch for these diagnostic symptoms:

  • N deficiency: pale green leaves, slow growth, small bulbs.
  • P deficiency: stunted plants, purplish leaf tips in seedlings.
  • K deficiency: leaf-tip dieback, poor bulb firmness, short storage life.
  • Ca deficiency: pale, translucent leaf tips; split bulbs.
  • S deficiency: pale yellow young leaves; low pungency.
  • Zn deficiency: banded chlorosis, narrow leaves.

6. Fertigation: Injecting Fertilizers via Irrigation

Fertigation is the highest-precision tool available to African onion growers with drip or micro-sprinkler systems, and it is increasingly used in commercial operations around Nairobi, Arusha, Addis Ababa's Rift Valley suppliers, and Moroccan-style export farms in Senegal. It delivers nutrients directly to the active root zone in small, frequent doses, improving fertilizer-use efficiency by 30â50% versus broadcasting. Soluble fertilizers used include urea, potassium nitrate, calcium nitrate, monoammonium phosphate, and complete water-soluble blends. Inject at 0.5â2.0 g/L, flush the lines with clean water after each cycle, and never mix calcium with phosphate or sulphate salts in the same tank â they precipitate and clog emitters.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Fertilizer Handling & Fertigation

Fertilizers are agricultural chemicals. Always wear gloves, goggles, and a face mask when handling or mixing. Store fertilizers away from children, livestock, food, and drinking water. Never mix calcium nitrate with phosphate or sulphate fertilizers in the same tank â the reaction produces insoluble precipitates that clog drip emitters and reduce nutrient availability. Do not apply nitrogen after 70 days from transplanting; late N delays maturity, causes thick necks, and destroys storage quality. Follow all national regulations on fertilizer registration and use (e.g., KEPHIS in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria, TOSCI in Tanzania).

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Soil test before planting; adjust lime or gypsum based on pH results.
  2. Apply all P and 60% of K as basal at transplanting.
  3. Split N into 2â3 applications; stop N by day 70 after transplanting.
  4. Use foliar Ca+B at bulb initiation to prevent split and thick-neck bulbs.
  5. Incorporate 10â20 t/ha well-decomposed manure or 5â10 t/ha compost.
  6. Rotate away from Allium crops for at least 2â3 seasons.
  7. If fertigating, flush lines after each injection and never mix Ca with P or S.
  8. Keep records of rates, dates, and yields to refine next season's programme.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Crop Information: Onion
  • Oregon State University Extension â Nutrient Management for Onions (PNW 709)
  • University of California ANR â Onion Production in California
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural & Livestock Research Organisation (horticulture resources)
  • AVRDC / World Vegetable Center â Onion & Shallot Production Guides

Prepared as part of the Rise Africa Skills course Onion Farming. Business-first: every recommendation here is intended to protect marketable yield, bulb quality, and storage life â the three variables that determine the price an African onion grower actually receives.

quiz.q: What is the approximate root depth of onion plants?
quiz.explanation: Onion roots are shallow, mostly in the top 15-20 cm of soil.

quiz.q: For a 1-hectare onion crop yielding 20-30 tonnes, how much nitrogen (N) is typically removed?
quiz.explanation: Onions remove roughly 100-120 kg N per hectare for that yield level.

quiz.q: When do onions take up nutrients most rapidly?
quiz.explanation: Rapid uptake occurs from about day 40 to day 80 as leaves and bulbs form.

quiz.q: Why is banding fertilizer better than broadcasting for onions?
options: B) Onions have small root volume
quiz.explanation: Band placement puts nutrients close to the limited root zone.

quiz.q: What happens if you apply too much nitrogen late in the season?
options: B) Thick necks and poor storage
quiz.explanation: Late nitrogen delays maturity and causes thick necks that rot in storage.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of split fertilizer applications?
options: B) Reduces nutrient loss and salt burn
quiz.explanation: Splitting reduces leaching and volatilization, and prevents salt damage to seedlings.

quiz.q: How many split applications are commonly recommended for onions?
quiz.explanation: Dividing total fertilizer into 2-4 parts matches the uptake curve.

quiz.q: What is a common basal fertilizer for onions?
quiz.explanation: NPK 15-15-15 provides a balanced start for onions.

quiz.q: How much urea would you apply to supply 46 kg N?
quiz.explanation: Urea is 46% N, so 100 kg urea gives 46 kg N.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid applying urea on wet onion leaves?
quiz.explanation: Urea on wet leaves can cause leaf burn.

quiz.q: What is foliar feeding?
options: B) Spraying liquid fertilizer on leaves
quiz.explanation: Foliar feeding means spraying nutrients directly onto leaves.

quiz.q: What concentration of urea solution is commonly used for foliar spray on onions?
quiz.explanation: A 2-3% urea solution (20-30 g per litre) is safe and effective.

quiz.q: When is the best time to spray foliar fertilizer?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
D) When leaves are dry and hot
quiz.explanation: Spraying in cooler hours reduces evaporation and leaf burn.

quiz.q: Why add soap to a foliar spray?
options: B) As a sticker to help spray stick
quiz.explanation: Soap acts as a surfactant, helping the spray adhere to waxy leaves.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes purple leaf tips in onions?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus deficiency often shows as purple leaf tips.

quiz.q: What is a good organic source of potassium for onions?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is rich in potassium and calcium.

quiz.q: How much well-rotted cattle manure is recommended per hectare for onions?
quiz.explanation: Apply 10-20 tonnes per hectare and incorporate before planting.

quiz.q: Why should fresh manure be composted before use?
options: B) To kill weed seeds and pathogens
C) To make it easier to spread
quiz.explanation: Composting kills weed seeds and pathogens and prevents root burn.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of combining organic and mineral fertilizers?
options: B) Higher yield and improved soil health
quiz.explanation: Integrated use provides balanced nutrition and builds soil.

quiz.q: What is biochar?
quiz.explanation: Biochar is charred organic matter that improves soil fertility and water retention.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil pH range for onions?
quiz.explanation: Onions grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, pH 6.0-6.8.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes yellowing between veins on older leaves?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium deficiency shows as interveinal chlorosis on older leaves.

quiz.q: What is a symptom of calcium deficiency in onions?
quiz.explanation: Calcium deficiency causes leaf tip dieback and poor bulb storage.

quiz.q: How much zinc sulphate is recommended if soil is deficient?
quiz.explanation: Apply 10-20 kg/ha of zinc sulphate to correct zinc deficiency.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation important for preventing nutrient deficiencies?
options: B) It balances nutrient use and reduces disease
quiz.explanation: Rotation with cereals or legumes helps balance nutrients and break pest cycles.

quiz.q: What is fertigation?
options: B) Injecting fertilizers into irrigation water
quiz.explanation: Fertigation is the injection of soluble fertilizers into irrigation water.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is NOT suitable for fertigation?
quiz.explanation: Granular fertilizers do not fully dissolve and can clog emitters.

quiz.q: Why should you flush the irrigation system after fertigation?
options: B) To prevent salt buildup in lines
quiz.explanation: Flushing with clean water prevents salt accumulation and clogging.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended EC for onion fertigation?
quiz.explanation: Keep EC below 2.0 dS/m to avoid salt burn in onions.

quiz.q: What is a common injector for small-scale fertigation?
quiz.explanation: A venturi injector is a simple, affordable device for injecting fertilizer.
